intro: John Michel opens Bach’s First Cello Suite with a single line that seems to carry its own bass. The bow circles through broken chords, then breaks free into scales before the final G-major chord.

sections.label: A · G major, one note at a time
sections.mNote: Broken chords circle above a changing bass

sections.label: B · Scales after the held D
sections.mNote: The cello runs on after the fermata

sections.label: Coda · A chromatic climb above D
sections.mNote: The upper notes rise towards the final G-major chord

cues.title: One cello, bass and melody
cues.text: G, D, B: the cello opens a G-major chord one note at a time. The low G keeps returning while the bow circles through the notes above it. With no accompanist, the cello supplies both the bass and everything that grows from it.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 1–4, in the Mutopia edition: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A held D, then flight
cues.text: A rising arpeggio reaches D and stops on a fermata. Then the cello starts running again, in scales that escape the opening’s repeated pattern. D belongs to the dominant of G; the home chord is still some way off.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bar 22 and following: fermata on D followed by freer semiquaver figuration. Mutopia edition, music ID 517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: D beneath the climb
cues.text: A repeated D alternates with a line climbing by semitones. The cello keeps touching that fixed note as the upper notes rise beyond it. After one last round of broken chords, the bow settles on a full G-major chord.
cues.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 37–42: chromatic ascent alternating with D, then broken chords and the final G-major chord. Mutopia edition, music ID 517.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The held D releases a scale
transitions.from: A · G major, one note at a time
transitions.to: B · Scales after the held D
transitions.how: The cello climbs to a D marked with a fermata. After the pause, semiquavers run up the scale and spread through a wider range. The bass and upper notes still belong to one bow; D, the dominant of G, keeps the ending in suspense.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bar 22 and following; Mutopia edition, music ID 517.

transitions.title: A fixed D, a climbing line
transitions.from: B · Scales after the held D
transitions.to: Coda · A chromatic climb above D
transitions.how: The cello alternates D with a rising chromatic line. The repeated note acts as a dominant pedal while the upper notes climb. Broken chords then lead through the final cadence to G major, held beneath a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer score (1916), Prelude, bars 37–42; Mutopia edition, music ID 517.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education.

In 1703 Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and married his second cousin Maria Barbara. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
